name: Email
title: ChatGPT prompts for email
description: Free copy-paste prompt templates for writing emails with ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini: replies, follow-ups, bad news and emails that sound like you.
intro: Each template fixes the parts that make AI emails go wrong — tone, length, and facts the model must not invent — and leaves named slots for what changes. Fill every [SLOT]. If you can't fill one, the email isn't ready to delegate yet.

templates.title: Reply in your own voice
templates.useWhen: You need a reply that does not sound like a template.
templates.prompt:
Write a reply to the email between <<< and >>>.
Goal of my reply: [WHAT I WANT TO HAPPEN NEXT]
My voice — match these two short emails I wrote: <<<[PASTE 2 EMAILS YOU SENT]>>>
Rules: under [120] words; no greetings or sign-offs I don't use in the samples; do not promise dates, prices or commitments that are not in my goal. If the email asks something my goal doesn't answer, list it as a question for me instead of guessing.

Email: <<<[PASTE EMAIL]>>>
templates.why: Real samples beat adjectives like “friendly but professional”. The no-promises rule stops the model inventing commitments you would then have to honour.

templates.title: Polite follow-up after no reply
templates.useWhen: Someone has not answered and you need a decision.
templates.prompt:
Write a follow-up email to [RECIPIENT ROLE] who has not replied to my message from [HOW LONG AGO].
Original message: <<<[PASTE]>>>
What I need from them: [ONE SPECIFIC ACTION] by [DATE].
Rules: three sentences maximum; restate the ask in the first sentence; make replying easy (a yes/no question or two options); no guilt-tripping phrases like “just circling back” or “as per my last email”.
templates.why: Follow-ups fail when the ask is buried. Fixing the length and putting the action first gives the reader a ten-second decision.

templates.title: Deliver bad news clearly
templates.useWhen: A delay, a refusal or a mistake has to be communicated.
templates.prompt:
Draft an email telling [AUDIENCE] that [THE BAD NEWS].
Facts I can confirm: [LIST THE FACTS]
What happens next / what they can do: [OPTIONS]
Rules: state the news in the first two sentences; one sentence of genuine acknowledgement, no over-apologising; do not speculate about causes beyond the facts above; end with the single next step. Give me two versions: one direct, one warmer.
templates.why: Burying bad news breeds distrust. The facts list bounds what the model may claim, and two versions let you choose the tone without re-prompting.

templates.title: Cut a long email in half
templates.useWhen: Your draft is too long and people stop reading.
templates.prompt:
Shorten the email between <<< and >>> to at most [HALF THE WORDS] words.
Keep: every date, number, name, and every request I make.
Cut: repetition, hedging, and background the reader already knows ([WHAT THEY KNOW]).
Then list, one line each, anything you removed that I might want back.

Email: <<<[PASTE DRAFT]>>>
templates.why: Shortening is where models silently drop facts. The keep-list protects them and the removal list makes the edit auditable.

templates.title: Ask a busy senior person for something
templates.useWhen: You need approval, time or a decision from someone with no time.
templates.prompt:
Write an email to [NAME, ROLE] asking for [THE REQUEST].
Context they need (and nothing more): [2–3 FACTS]
Why it matters to them: [THEIR INTEREST, NOT MINE]
Rules: subject line under 8 words that states the ask; first line = the ask; under 100 words in total; offer the smallest possible yes (for example a 15-minute call or a one-word approval).
templates.why: Senior readers triage by subject line and first sentence. The template forces the ask to the top and frames it in their interest.

templates.title: Translate an email and keep the tone
templates.useWhen: You write to someone in another language or country.
templates.prompt:
Translate the email between <<< and >>> into [LANGUAGE] for a reader in [COUNTRY OR REGION].
Keep: the level of formality ([FORMAL / NEUTRAL / CASUAL]) and all names, numbers, dates and product names exactly.
Adapt: greetings, sign-offs and idioms to what a native speaker would actually write.
After the translation, list any phrase where the literal meaning and the natural phrasing differed, so I can check it.

Email: <<<[PASTE]>>>
templates.why: Literal translation reads as foreign; free translation drifts. Naming what to keep and what to adapt, plus the flagged phrases, keeps you in control.
